skills.content:
Approach this as the design lead at a small studio known for their versatility, giving every client a visual identity pitched at the treatment the task actually calls for. Make deliberate choices about palette, typography, and layout that are specific to this subject, and avoid templated designs.

## Read the request first

Calibrate treatment, not whether to design. A doc deserves the same craft as a landing page — what changes is the treatment that craft is delivered in.

Many requests call for a more utilitarian treatment: a plan, a memo, a demo. Make it polished: include real typographic hierarchy, considered spacing, and a proper palette, but avoid over-designing. Most pages do not need a flashy, gigantic hero. Keep flourishes tasteful and limited.

Some requests call for an editorial treatment: a landing page, a game, an app or tool they'll keep or share.

When unsure: a well-composed page is never the wrong answer; an over-designed visual identity sometimes is.

Fundamentals below apply to everything. The editorial process after that runs only when the read above says so.

## Fundamentals for every artifact

**Honor what's already there** Look for an existing design system first — CLAUDE.md, a tokens or theme file, existing component styles. When one exists, apply it; everything below fills gaps and never overrides. Precedence is always: the user's own words, then the project's existing system, then your choices.

**Ground it in the subject.** If the subject isn't already clear, pin it: one concrete subject, its audience, and the page's single job. The subject's own world — its materials, instruments, vernacular — is where distinctive choices come from. Build with real content throughout, never lorem.

**Pair typefaces** Typography carries the page even when the page isn't about typography. The Artifact CSP blocks font CDNs, so don't link a webfont URL and risk a silent fallback. Instead inline the face as a @font-face data URI. Keep running text near 65 characters wide; set a type scale and stay on it; give headings `text-wrap: balance`, body text room to breathe, and uppercase labels a touch of letter-spacing.

**Choose neutrals, don't default to them.** A pure mid-grey reads as unconsidered; a grey with a slight hue bias toward the page's accent reads as chosen. Pure white and near-black are fine grounds when they suit the subject — the point is that the neutral was picked, not inherited.

**Design both themes.** The page renders in the viewer's theme: `prefers-color-scheme` carries the OS preference, and the viewer's toggle stamps `data-theme="dark"` / `data-theme="light"` on the root element, which must override the media query in both directions. The robust pattern is token-level: define the palette as custom properties on `:root`, redefine only the tokens under `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` — style components through the tokens, never directly inside the media query — then redefine them again under `:root[data-theme="dark"]` and `:root[data-theme="light"]`. Give the second theme the same care as the first — don't naively invert; keep contrast legible and the accent working on both grounds. A design that deliberately commits to one visual world (a neon arcade screen, a letterpress invitation) may stay single-theme — make it a choice, not an omission.

**Let layout do the spacing.** Lay out sibling groups with flex or grid and `gap`, not per-element margins that silently collapse or double. Wide content — tables, code, diagrams — gets `overflow-x: auto` on its own container so the page body never scrolls sideways. Reach for `font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums` wherever digits line up in columns.

**Avoid AI-generated design** AI-generated design currently clusters around a few looks: warm cream (#F4F1EA) with a serif display and terracotta accent; near-black with a lone acid-green or vermilion pop; broadsheet hairline rules with dense columns; a purple-to-blue gradient hero on white; Inter or Space Grotesk as the "safe" face; emoji as section markers; everything centered; `rounded-lg` everywhere; accent bar/rail on rounded cards. Where the user pins down a visual direction, follow it exactly — their words always win, including when they ask for one of these looks. Where nothing is specified, don't spend that freedom on one of these defaults.

**Build cleanly** Be cognizant of overlapping elements, cascade collisions, silent font fallbacks; visual bugs hide in the gap between source and output. Close every non-void element, double-quote attributes, give keyboard focus a visible state, respect `prefers-reduced-motion`. For generative or decorative graphics, reach for Canvas or WebGL rather than hand-authoring long SVG path data.

**CSS rules** When writing the CSS, watch your selector specificities. It is easy to generate classes that cancel each other out — a type-based selector like `.section` fighting an element-based one like `.cta` over padding and margins between sections. Structure the cascade so it doesn't silently undo your spacing.

**Writing the copy** Words are design material, not decoration. Write from the user's side of the screen — name things by what people recognize, not how the system is built (a person manages *notifications*, not *webhook config*). Active voice; a control says exactly what happens ("Publish", then a toast that says "Published"). Errors explain what went wrong and how to fix it — no apologies, no vagueness. Specific beats clever.

**Structure is information** Structural devices, numbering, eyebrows, dividers, labels, should encode something true about the content, not decorate it. Many generic designs use numbered markers (01 / 02 / 03), but that's only appropriate if the content actually is a sequence - like a real process or a typed timeline where order carries information the reader needs. Question if choices like numbered markers actually make sense before incorporating them.

**When it's a UI, not a document** A dashboard or tool is scanned and operated, not read top-to-bottom, so the craft shifts from typography to information design. Surface the summary before the detail; encode state in form as well as number — a pill, a chip, a severity stripe — so what needs attention reads at a glance. Semantic color (good / warning / critical) is separate from the accent hue and doesn't count as your accent. Give sparklines and charts the same care as type: an area fill, a faint grid, an emphasized endpoint. What's interactive should look interactive.



## Process

Before writing code, sketch a short design plan — a compact token system with color, type, and layout:
- **Color**: describe the palette as 4–6 named hex values.
- **Type**: typefaces for 2+ roles — a characterful display face used with restraint, a complementary body face, and a utility face for captions or data if needed.
- **Layout**: a layout concept in one or two sentences.

Then build, following the plan and deriving every color and type decision from it.

## When the request is editorial

The stance shifts: the client has already rejected proposals that felt templated, and is paying for a distinctive point of view. Make opinionated calls, and take one real aesthetic risk where it serves the work.

Review the design plan against the subject before building: if any part of it reads like the generic default you would produce for any similar page, revise that part, and note what you changed and why. Only after you've confirmed the plan's uniqueness do you write the code, following the revised plan exactly.

**Principles** 

- The hero is a thesis: open with the most characteristic thing in the subject's world — headline, image, live demo, interactive moment. 
- Typography carries the personality of the page. Pair the display and body faces deliberately, not the same families you would reach for on any other project, and set a clear type scale with intentional weights, widths, and spacing. Make the type treatment itself a memorable part of the design, not a neutral delivery vehicle for the content. 
- Leverage motion deliberately. Think about where and if animation can serve the subject: a page-load sequence, a scroll-triggered reveal, hover micro-interactions, ambient atmosphere. An orchestrated moment usually lands harder than scattered effects; choose what the direction calls for. However, sometimes less is more, and extra animation contributes to the feeling that the design is AI-generated. 
- Match complexity to the vision. Maximalist directions need elaborate execution; minimal directions need precision in spacing, type, and detail. Elegance is executing the chosen vision well.
- Spend your boldness in one place; keep everything around it quiet. If the accent fights the ground, shift it toward analogous or drop saturation rather than replacing it.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Hybrid K=51 ROI cycle measurement for the prefetch reproduce runbook
# (q1_0_hvm_reproduce.md). Prints, per binary, the [roi] self-check line
# (now including nrows) and the [andesim] <N> cycles figure for the K=51 node.
#
#   bash measure.sh                     # pristine baseline prefetch (gemv/decode node)
#   bash measure.sh baseline prefetch   # just the prefetch A/B
#   PROMPT="The capital of France" WARMUP=--no-warmup bash measure.sh baseline prefetch
#                                       # pure-gemm node (nrows=4): measures the gemm path
#
# GEMV (decode) node = the warmup forward pass, nrows=2. Expected K=51 cycles:
#   pristine 4,476,168 -> baseline 2,144,213 -> prefetch 1,391,650
#   (prefetch = 1.54x vs baseline, 3.22x vs pristine)
# GEMM (prefill) node = --no-warmup + a 4-token prompt, nrows=4 (pure gemm):
#   baseline 1,696,704 -> prefetch 1,649,275 (only 1.03x - gemm reuses each
#   weight block across the M-tile of 4, so it is ~compute-bound, little to hide)
#   pristine 8,875,248 -> prefetch 1,651,949 -> d4 931,754 -> d4+F9 818,314
#   (10.85x over pristine). K=56 ffn_down: prefetch 13,474,132 -> d4 6,636,852
#   -> d4+F9 5,683,029. d4 beats prefetch by more on ffn_down (2.03x vs 1.77x)
#   because 3.5 MB does not fit the 2 MB L3, so weight reuse still buys memory
#   traffic there.
#   Decode for comparison: pristine 4,476,673 -> prefetch 1,389,236 ->
#   d4 457,092 -> d4+F9 362,799 (12.34x over pristine).
#
#
# Other shapes: the measured node is compile-time (see build.sh ROI_K), so a
# shape sweep passes the suffixed binaries, e.g.
#   bash measure.sh pristine-k54 baseline-k54 prefetch-k54   # blk.7.ffn_gate
# Bonsai-4B has 6 distinct Q1_0 shapes; layer 7 covers all of them at
# ROI_K = 50 attn_q / 51 attn_v / 52 attn_k / 53 attn_output / 54 ffn_gate /
# 55 ffn_up / 56 ffn_down. Cost scales with rows*K, so ffn_* is ~9.5x the
# attn_v node -> raise TIMEOUT for those.
#
# Slow: the RTL leg runs at a few kHz -> minutes per binary. Override via env
# LLAMA / ANDESIM / MODEL / ENGINE / PROMPT / WARMUP / TIMEOUT.
set -e
export TMPDIR=${TMPDIR:-/home/nick/tmp}
LLAMA=${LLAMA:-/home/nick/work/llama.cpp}
ANDESIM=${ANDESIM:-/home/nick/work/andesim}
MODEL=${MODEL:-$LLAMA/models/Bonsai-4B-Q1_0.gguf}
ENGINE=${ENGINE:-vsim:ax46mpv_fpga_l3}
PROMPT=${PROMPT:-The capital of France is}
WARMUP=${WARMUP:-}
TIMEOUT=${TIMEOUT:-14400000}   # hybrid per-leg spawn timeout, ms (4h)

for b in ${*:-pristine baseline prefetch}; do
  echo "=== $b ==="
  ( cd "$ANDESIM" && ./andesim run --mode hybrid --trigger marker --runtime linux \
      --mem-size 2000M --engine "$ENGINE" --step-timeout-ms "$TIMEOUT" \
      "$LLAMA/bin-$b" -- -m "$MODEL" -no-cnv $WARMUP --prompt "$PROMPT" \
      -n 32 -c 512 -t 1 ) 2>&1 | grep -E '\[roi\]|\[andesim\] .*cycles'
done

# RISC-V Kernel Optimization Roadmap (Bonsai-4B Q1_0 / Ternary Q2_0)

Primary model: models/Bonsai-4B-Q1_0.gguf (572 MB, arch qwen3, 36 layers,
embd 2560, GQA with 1024-wide K/V projections, 253 MUL_MAT nodes per token
= 36 x 7 + lm_head).

Why 4B (decision 2026-07-21, replaces the old 27B focus):
- Fits andesim hybrid's hard 2 GiB guest-RAM cap with room for KV cache and
  compute buffers (27B needs ~4.5 GB - blocked until andesim grows >2 GiB
  DRAM support).
- Plain qwen3: output is coherent on rv64. The qwen35 hybrid-attention bug
  (old F0) only affects 27B, so it no longer blocks anything - parked below.
- The full closed loop already works on 4B: end-to-end cycle-accurate
  per-kernel measurement under andesim hybrid marker mode was confirmed
  2026-07-16 (see Measurement setup).

Hardware targets (both vsim engines, VLEN 512-2048 family per F4 design):
- vsim:ax45mpv_premium - VLEN=512, DLEN=512, ELEN=32, no zfh/zvfh.
- vsim:ax46mpv_fpga_l3 - VLEN=1024, ELEN=64, first engine with real L3.

Baselines:
- QEMU proxy (insn-count, -t 8, build-rv64-noomp, 2026-07-15):
  4B ~19-21 s/token. QEMU time tracks instruction count, not latency.
- Real cycles, hybrid marker ROI at K=51 (layer 7 V projection, 2560x1024,
  the smallest matmul in the model - nothing smaller exists per-layer):
  - ax45mpv_premium: 6528953 cycles (2026-07-16, stable across runs)
  - ax46mpv_fpga_l3: 4476168 cycles (2026-07-16, pristine upstream ggml)
  These are THE per-kernel before/after gate for F1-F7: same K, same model,
  real pipeline + memory system.

Rules for every feature below:
- TDD: first add a correctness test comparing the new kernel against the
  matching *_generic function on random data (test-quantize-fns style),
  see it fail/pass, then optimize. Never commit a kernel without the test.
- Benchmark gate: QEMU proxy for correctness + rough insn counts, then
  hybrid marker ROI cycles before/after (the real number). FPGA only for
  final full-token figures.

ELEN=32 constraint (ax45mpv_premium): no 64-bit vector elements anywhere.
Stock repack.cpp uses __riscv_vsseg4e64 -> GGML_CPU_REPACK=OFF today; any
new F4 kernel must stay e32-clean (the Nx1 design already is: vlm masks,
int16 sumi, fp32 accumulators). Also: premium's FP datapath rejects LMUL=8
float ops (integer LMUL=8 is fine) - F4's VLEN=512 -> m4 fp32 mapping is
exactly at the safe limit; never use m8 for float.

Status legend: TODO / IN-PROGRESS / DONE / PARKED

---

## F1. Q1_0 multi-row vec_dot (nrows = 2)

- Status: TODO
- Description: The Q1_0 dot kernel recomputes/reloads the same activations
  for every weight row. Set `.nrows = 2` (later 4) so one call computes 2
  output elements: load + negate activations once, per row only do mask
  load (vlm) + vmerge + reduce. Expected ~1.5-2x on the dominant matmul path.
- Gate: K=51 ROI cycles before/after (V projection is exactly this path).
- Key files:
  - ggml/src/ggml-cpu/arch/riscv/quants.c:484-578 (vl256/vl128 kernels + dispatcher)
  - ggml/src/ggml-cpu/ggml-cpu.c:227-232 (.nrows field of GGML_TYPE_Q1_0)

nds.vd4dots.vv is a stock Andes vendor instruction, not a custom ACE extension. At e32 it computes, for every 32-bit lane:

vd[j] += vs1[4j+0]*vs2[4j+0] + vs1[4j+1]*vs2[4j+1] + vs1[4j+2]*vs2[4j+2] + vs1[4j+3]*vs2[4j+3] ; int8 x int8 accumulated into the i32 lane ; vd, vs1, vs2 all at the same LMUL

At VLEN=1024, e32/m2 is exactly 64 i32 lanes = 64 rows, and that same register group seen as bytes is 256 bytes = 64 rows x 4 columns. The instruction's operand shape and the repacked tile are the same object. The only work left was to make the bits arrive in that order.

Lane j is output row j. Its four bytes are that row's four consecutive K columns. One instruction retires 64 rows x 4 columns = 256 MACs.

Bit index (c/4)*256 + 4*j + (c%4). A plane now covers four columns. Bit 4j + (c%4) is byte lane 4j + (c%4) of the register group — the position the dot reads for row j, column c. Same bytes as stage 02, only permuted.

one vlm 32 B mask ... 64 nibbles

Read as 64 nibbles: nibble j is row j, and its four bits are columns c..c+3. A single vmerge turns the whole mask into 256 bytes of +1 / -1.

Same bytes, a quarter of the load operations. That is why the in-model win (3.04x) beats the standalone cache-resident lab (2.52x) — the lab could not see the load traffic.

One authority

The layout cannot drift

Both bit orders live in one function, q1_0x64_sign_bit(). The repack writer and every reader call it. A numeric test can never catch a layout mistake here — writer and reader share the bug, so it cancels. Only a codegen gate can.

gemv activation side

Restage, do not gather

The dot wants 4 activation quants as one 32-bit element, but block_q8_0 puts qs at offset 2, so every other group is 2 mod 4 and the core faults on a misaligned 32-bit vector element load. Copy the quants once per call through byte load/store (EEW=8 has no alignment rule). Under 1%.

gemm activation side

De-interleave with vnsrl

The x4 activation block stores qs[c*4 + m], but row m needs its four columns contiguous — a stride-4 gather. Instead peel the byte lanes apart once per row tile with vnsrl (u32 to 2x u16 to 4x u8): 6 shifts and 4 stores per 32 columns, reused by every column tile.

The two tiles

Same instruction, mirrored

Decode multiplies by one activation vector; prefill by four at once. The dot is used the same way in both, but which operand is reused flips — and that decides how the registers are budgeted.

gemv / decodeq1_vd4dots_x4_m2
weights
activations
accumulator

Four different columns, one accumulator. Four dots are chained into the same register so the pipeline stays fed while each result is still in flight.

gemm / prefillq1_vd4dots_4acc_m2
weights
activations
accumulators

One weight vector, four output rows. The weight stream is read once and used four times, which is why prefill was already efficient before stage 03 and gained little from prefetching.

=== F9 tail ===
## F9. Q1_0 d4 kernels: kill the vtype churn - DONE 2026-08-01

- Status: DONE and shipped in the same Q1_D4 build. Decode 1.26x, prefill
  1.14-1.17x on top of F8.
- The problem, from the F8 O3 assembly: the kernels alternate between the byte
  view (vlm mask load, vmerge sign expand) and the 32-bit view (vmv.v.x
  broadcast, the dot). Every alternation needs a vsetvli, which does no
  arithmetic. 4 per dot in the gemv - 40% of its inner loop. GCC's share is
  that it cannot see inside an inline asm block, so it assumes each one left
  vtype unknown and re-issues its own on top of the one in the block.
- WHAT DID NOT WORK, worth knowing: grouping the two widths in the SOURCE
  (all 4 vlm+vmerge, then all 4 broadcast+dot). The scheduler interleaves them
  again and it only got the gemv from 4.00 to 2.00 vsetvli per dot.
  What works is putting everything at e32 INSIDE one asm block - the
  broadcasts included - so GCC only ever has e8 work to schedule.
  Side benefit: taking the activation quads as uint32 GPRs and writing
  vmv.v.x by hand makes the vlse32 stride-0 trap impossible by construction,
  so q1_bcast_act4 and its barrier are gone.
- ALSO DID NOT WORK: 4 scratch activation registers instead of 2, to double
  the distance between each vmv.v.x and the dot that consumes it. No spills,
  4.06 vs 4.13 instrs/dot - and 855,476 cycles vs 818,314, i.e. 4.5% WORSE.
  The producer-consumer distance is not what limits the gemm. Reverted.
- STATIC (O3, between the first and last dot):
      vsetvli per dot   gemv 4.00 -> 0.94     gemm 2.00 -> 0.52
      instrs per dot    gemv 10.00 -> 7.90    gemm 9.00 -> 4.13
  The gemm gains more because the smaller body also let GCC unroll its column
  loop 8x, which it would not do before. No vector spills in either.
- MEASURED, same engine and cmdline as F8:
      node                        F8          F9    F9/F8   vs pristine
      K=51 decode  nrows=2    457,092     362,799    1.26x    12.34x
      K=51 prefill nrows=4    931,754     818,314    1.14x    10.85x
      K=56 prefill nrows=4  6,636,852   5,683,029    1.17x        -
- THE INTERESTING PART - decode and prefill are now bound by different things.
  Cycles per issued instruction (cycles / dots / instrs-per-dot):
      gemv   F8 2.23  ->  F9 2.24     unchanged
      gemm   F8 2.53  ->  F9 4.84     nearly doubled
  The gemv is purely instruction-issue bound: its cost per instruction did not
  move, so F9 converted the instruction saving straight into cycles, 1:1. That
  also means F8's "instruction-issue floor" of 328,865 (measured with HVM) was
  never a floor - it was an instruction count, and F9 beat it at 362,799 with
  no HVM at all.
  The gemm is NOT issue bound any more. At the gemv's 2.24 cyc/instr its 4.13
  instructions per dot should cost ~9.2 cycles; it costs 20.0. So ~11 cycles
  per dot are stall, and cutting instructions further will not help prefill.
  Both kernels now sit at 17.7 (gemv) and 20.0 (gemm) cycles per
  nds.vd4dots.vv, which is suspicious enough to suspect the instruction's own
  throughput at e32/m2 - but that is NOT established.
  THE EXPERIMENT THAT WOULD SETTLE IT, not yet run: d4-nopf and d4-hvm on the
  PREFILL node (both build targets already exist; ~25 min including builds).
  If prefetch-off and HVM both leave it near 818,314, the limit is the dot
  rate and prefill is done until the ISA changes. If HVM moves it, the limit
  is the 4 activation streams plus the weight stream, and the fix is software.
- Key files: arch/riscv/repack.cpp `q1_vd4dots_x4_m2` (gemv: 4 pairs into one
  accumulator) and `q1_vd4dots_4acc_m2` (gemm: one weight against the 4 rows
  of the M-tile). Gate: ./check-vd4dots.sh, VTYPE-CHURN budget of 1 vsetvli
  per dot, which fails on the F8 code at O3 and passes now.
- Correctness: bit-identical, not just close - test-repack-q1_0 13/13 with
  every nmse unchanged from the F8 run, at Q1_D4=1 and Q1_D4=0.

---

## Measurement setup (fixed for all features)

Three-tier ladder - each feature climbs it in order:

1. Correctness (host + QEMU):
   - New-kernel test vs *_generic, random tensors, tolerance 0 for integer
     paths / 1 ulp for float accumulation-order changes.
   - Standalone kernel lab: kernel-lab/ builds Q1_0 kernels outside ggml
     (make host / make rv64 / make asm), bit-exact vs generic + double-ref
     gate + --inject self-test; QEMU at vlen=512/256/128 via
     run-rv64-qemu.sh. Correctness only - no timing code in the harness.
     Iterate here first, then paste back into
     ggml/src/ggml-cpu/arch/riscv/quants.c and re-verify test-quantize-fns.
   - QEMU proxy limits (measured 2026-07-16): qemu-user TCG cost is
     dominated by per-vector-instruction helper overhead; scalar insns are
     ~free and stalls do not exist. It rewards fewer vector instructions and
     punishes stall-removal restructures even when they win on hardware
     (the lesson that killed F2). Correctness + rough insn counts ONLY.
   - QEMU proxy bench: ./run-rv64-qemu.sh llama-bench -m
     models/Bonsai-4B-Q1_0.gguf -p 8 -n 4 -r 1 -t 8
     (BIN_DIR=build-rv64-noomp/bin; llama-cli unusable under QEMU - use

    </p>
  </div>
</header>

<!-- ============ THE MACHINE ============ -->
<section class="sec" id="machine">
  <div class="wrap">
    <div class="sec-head">
      <p class="eyebrow">Where this runs</p>
      <h2>One core, one wide vector unit, no L2</h2>
      <div class="prose">
        <p>
          The target is an <strong>Andes AX46MPV</strong> RISC-V core. It is not silicon yet:
          it is RTL, simulated cycle by cycle. That is the single fact that shapes everything
          below. Nothing here is guessed from a model of the pipeline, and nothing here is a
          wall-clock time either — the simulator runs at a few kHz, so every number on
          this page is a <strong>cycle count</strong>.
        </p>
        <p>
          Two properties of this core drive every decision. The vector unit is
          <strong>wide</strong> — 1024 bits, so 128 int8 lanes in one register — and
          the memory system behind it is <strong>thin</strong>: 32 KB of L1 data cache, no L2 at
          all, and a 2 MB L3. A kernel that keeps the lanes busy wins twice, because it also
          spends fewer trips through that memory system.
        </p>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="panels two">
      <div class="panel">
        <div class="panel-label"><span>The core</span><span class="r">vsim:ax46mpv_fpga_l3</span></div>
        <dl class="spec">
          <dt>harts</dt><dd class="warn">1</dd>
          <dt>VLEN / DLEN</dt><dd>1024 / 1024 bit</dd>
          <dt>ELEN</dt><dd>64 bit</dd>
          <dt>L1 I / L1 D</dt><dd>32 KB / 32 KB, 4-way</dd>
          <dt>L2</dt><dd class="warn">none</dd>
          <dt>L3</dt><dd>2 MB, 4 banks</dd>
          <dt>cache line</dt><dd>64 B</dd>
          <dt>D-cache prefetch entries</dt><dd class="warn">4</dd>
          <dt>L3 line prefetch</dt><dd class="warn">off</dd>
        </dl>
        <p class="cap">
          Read from the engine's own config, <code>ax46mpv_fpga_l3.cfg</code>. <b>One hart</b> is
          why every run on this page passes <code>-t 1</code>, and why "just use more threads"
          is never an answer here.
        </p>
      </div>
      <div class="panel">
        <div class="panel-label"><span>The model</span><span class="r">Bonsai-4B-Q1_0.gguf</span></div>
        <dl class="spec">
          <dt>architecture</dt><dd>qwen3, 36 layers</dd>
          <dt>embedding / FFN width</dt><dd>2560 / 9728</dd>
          <dt>heads (Q / KV)</dt><dd>32 / 8</dd>
          <dt>Q1_0 tensors</dt><dd>253</dd>
          <dt>Q1_0 weights</dt><dd>4.02 G</dd>
          <dt>file on disk</dt><dd>572 MB</dd>
          <dt>output projection</dt><dd><em>tied to</em> token_embd</dd>
        </dl>
        <p class="cap">
          253 Q1_0 tensors is exactly <b>36 layers x 7 + 1</b>. The +1 is the LM head, and it is
          a single tensor holding <b>9.7% of all the weights in the model</b>. Keep it in mind;
          it decides the ending.
        </p>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="prose" style="margin-top:2rem">
      <p>
        Producing one token means running all 253 of those matmuls. Norms, RoPE, softmax and
        sampling are also there, but next to 4.02 G weight-multiplies they are rounding error.
        <strong>Speeding up this model means speeding up one function.</strong>
      </p>
      <p>
        That function runs in two different shapes, and they behave differently enough that
        every number on this page is reported twice:
      </p>
    </div>

    <div class="panels two">
      <div class="panel">
        <div class="panel-label"><span>Decode</span><span class="r">gemv, one column</span></div>
        <p class="cap" style="margin-top:0">
          Generating text, one token at a time. The weight matrix is multiplied by a
          <b>single activation vector</b>. Every weight is read from memory, used once, and
          thrown away — so this shape is naturally starved for memory bandwidth.
        </p>
      </div>
      <div class="panel">
        <div class="panel-label"><span>Prefill</span><span class="r">gemm, four columns</span></div>
        <p class="cap" style="margin-top:0">
          Reading the prompt, many tokens at once. The same weight matrix is multiplied by
          <b>four activation vectors</b> at a time, so each weight that arrives is used four
          times. More arithmetic per byte loaded, and a different bottleneck.
        </p>
      </div>
    </div>
    <p class="cap" style="max-width:74ch">
      ggml picks between them on the spot: more than three columns of activations goes to the
      gemm, the leftovers go to the gemv. Both read the exact same weight bytes, so any change
      to the layout has to serve both.
    </p>
  </div>
</section>

<!-- ============ METHOD ============ -->
<section class="sec" id="method">
  <div class="wrap">
    <div class="sec-head">
      <p class="eyebrow">How we measure</p>
      <h2>Count one node, not one token</h2>
      <div class="prose">
        <p>
          An RTL simulation is far too slow to generate a token end to end and time it. So we
          do not. <strong>andesim hybrid mode</strong> runs the whole program on a fast
          functional model, and when the program hits a marker it hands the machine state over
          to the RTL engine, which counts real cycles until the closing marker.
        </p>
        <p>
          The markers sit around <strong>one MUL_MAT node</strong>, picked at compile time.
          Nothing else in the model can pollute the number, and the same node can be re-measured
          for every build. Every stage below is a separately built binary run with an identical
          command line.
        </p>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="panels two">
      <div class="panel">
        <div class="panel-label"><span>Inside the measured window</span><span class="r">paid on every token</span></div>
        <ul class="tick">
          <li>Quantizing the activations from float down to 8-bit. <b>The baseline pays this
            too</b>, so the comparison is like for like.</li>
          <li>Expanding the 64 fp16 row scales to fp32, once per weight block.</li>
          <li>Restaging or de-interleaving the activation quants, from stage 04 on.</li>
          <li>The gemv or gemm itself.</li>
        </ul>
      </div>
      <div class="panel">
        <div class="panel-label"><span>Outside it</span><span class="r">paid once, at model load</span></div>
        <ul class="tick out">
          <li><b>The weight repack.</b> It runs inside the buffer's <code>set_tensor</code>
            while the model file is being read, before any graph executes. The ROI markers are
            not armed yet.</li>
        </ul>
        <p class="cap">
          Not measured on the target, but bounded from the generated code. The repack loop is
          scalar and runs <b>once per weight bit</b>: extract the bit, compute the destination
          index, read-modify-write one byte. Compiled for rv64 at <code>-O2</code> that inner
          loop is <b>16 instructions per bit</b> in the stage 02 order and <b>21 in the stage 04
          order</b>, with no unrolling.
        </p>
        <div class="tally" style="margin-top:.7rem">
          <dt>Q1_0 weights in the model</dt><dd>4.02 G</dd>
          <dt>fails the repack gate (LM head)</dt><dd>9.7%</dd>
          <dt>actually repacked</dt><dd>3.63 G</dd>
          <dt>instructions, single-threaded</dt><dd class="lo">76 G</dd>
          <dt>one optimized decode pass</dt><dd>1.27 G cycles</dd>
        </div>
        <p class="cap">
          That is a real cost and it lands entirely on time-to-first-token — on the order
          of a hundred tokens of payback. The same loop takes 4.5 s on an x86 host, where
          out-of-order execution hides the read-modify-write chain; this core cannot.
        </p>
        <p class="cap">
          It is also fixable, and nobody has tried: <b>cache the repacked buffer on disk</b> so
          it becomes a build step, or <b>vectorize the bit transpose</b> using the same mask
          operations the kernel itself uses. Splitting it across threads is <b>not</b> an option
          on this engine — it has one hart.
        </p>
      </div>
    </div>

    <ul class="kv">
      <li>
        <span class="k">Measured node</span>
        <span class="v"><code>blk.7.attn_v.weight</code>, K=2560, 1024 output rows — the
        smallest matmul in the model. Layer 7 also happens to contain all six distinct Q1_0
        shapes, so the whole layer can be swept.</span>
      </li>
      <li>
        <span class="k">Correctness</span>
        <span class="v">13 shape cases in <code>tests/test-repack-q1_0</code>, run against both
        layout orders. Stages 03, 04 and 05 are <b>bit-identical</b> to stage 02, not merely
        within tolerance.</span>
      </li>
      <li>
        <span class="k">What is not here</span>
        <span class="v">Tokens per second, and any statement about a clock frequency. Neither
        is knowable from an RTL run, so neither is claimed.</span>
      </li>
    </ul>
  </div>
</section>

<!-- ============ PROBLEM ============ -->
<section class="sec" id="problem">
  <div class="wrap">
    <div class="sec-head">
      <p class="eyebrow">The problem</p>
      <h2>A multiply that is not a multiply</h2>
      <div class="prose">
        <p>
          A Q1_0 block holds <strong>128 weights in 16 bytes</strong>, one bit each, plus one
          fp16 scale. Bit set means +1, bit clear means -1. The activations are Q8_0: 32 int8
          quants and one fp16 scale.
        </p>
        <p>
          So the inner operation is not a multiply-accumulate. It is <strong>add or subtract
          the activation</strong>. There is no arithmetic left to optimize. The entire cost of
          this kernel is decided by two questions: <strong>how many lanes are doing useful
          work</strong>, and <strong>how many instructions it takes to feed them</strong>.
        </p>
        <p>
          The stock kernel answers both badly, and it is not a tuning problem. The weight
          layout it inherits from the file format forces the answer.
        </p>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="panels two">
      <div class="panel">
        <div class="panel-label"><span>Weights — block_q1_0</span><span class="r">18 B</span></div>
        <div class="bytemap">
          <div class="bseg d" style="flex:2"><span>d</span><span class="n">fp16</span></div>
          <div class="bseg q striped" style="flex:16"><span>qs[16] — 128 sign bits</span><span class="n">bit c = column c</span></div>
        </div>
        <div class="bytemap-key"><span>byte 0</span><span>byte 17</span></div>
        <p class="cap">One block is <b>one row, 128 columns</b>. Rows sit one after another in memory.</p>
      </div>
      <div class="panel">
        <div class="panel-label"><span>Activations — block_q8_0</span><span class="r">34 B</span></div>
        <div class="bytemap">
          <div class="bseg d" style="flex:2"><span>d</span><span class="n">fp16</span></div>
          <div class="bseg q striped" style="flex:32"><span>qs[32] — int8 quants</span><span class="n">one byte per column</span></div>
        </div>
        <div class="bytemap-key"><span>byte 0</span><span>byte 33</span></div>
        <p class="cap"><b>qs starts at offset 2.</b> Remember this: it becomes a hardware fault in stage 04.</p>
      </div>
    </div>
  </div>
</section>

<!-- ============ STAGE 01 ============ -->
<section class="sec" id="s01">
  <div class="wrap">
    <div class="stage-head">
      <div class="stage-num">01</div>
      <div class="stage-titles">
        <p class="stage-kicker">Upstream baseline — ggml_vec_dot_q1_0_q8_0</p>
        <h2>One row at a time, and a reduction every 32 columns</h2>
        <div class="stage-cyc">
          <span class="chip">decode <b>4,476,168</b></span>
          <span class="chip">prefill <b>8,875,248</b></span>
          <span class="chip">1.00x, the starting point</span>
        </div>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="prose" style="margin-top:1.6rem">
      <p>
        Because a block is one row of 128 columns, the natural kernel loads part of one row,
        multiplies it against the activations, and adds the results together. That last step is
        the problem: adding up numbers that live in different lanes of the same vector register
        is a <strong>horizontal reduction</strong>, and it is serial.
      </p>
    </div>

    <div class="panels wide-left">
      <div class="panel">
        <div class="panel-label"><span>What one step touches</span><span class="r">1 row x 32 columns</span></div>
        <div class="gridbox">
          <div class="gridwrap">
            <div class="xlab"><span>col c</span><span>c+15 of 128</span></div>
            <div class="ylab"><span>row 0</span><span>row 63</span></div>
            <div class="lanegrid dim" data-rows="64" data-cols="16" data-seed="11"
                 data-hl="row" data-hl-start="9" data-hl-span="1" data-hl-tag="32 columns, 1 output"></div>
          </div>
        </div>
        <div class="legend">
          <span><i class="p"></i> weight +1</span>
          <span><i class="m"></i> weight -1</span>
          <span><i class="k"></i> one inner-loop step</span>
        </div>
        <p class="cap">
          The vector register holds <b>32 columns of a single row</b>. 63 of the 64 rows in this
          picture are idle while that one row is computed.
        </p>
      </div>

      <div class="panel">
        <div class="panel-label"><span>Inner loop</span><span class="r">per 32 columns</span></div>
        <div class="ops"><span class="cm">; VLMAX at e8m1 is 128 lanes; this uses 32</span>
<span class="op">vsetvl  </span>  e8, m1, vl=32
<span class="op">vlm.v   </span>  v0, (x.qs)      <span class="cm">; 32 sign bits</span>
<span class="op">vle8.v  </span>  v8, (y.qs)      <span class="cm">; 32 activations</span>
<span class="op">vneg.v  </span>  v9, v8
<span class="op">vmerge  </span>  v10, v9, v8, v0 <span class="cm">; +-y</span>
<span class="bad">vwredsum</span>  v11, v10, zero  <span class="cm">; horizontal !</span>
<span class="op">fmadd   </span>  acc, d_y, v11[0]</div>
        <dl class="tally">
          <dt>lanes busy</dt><dd class="lo">32 of 128</dd>
          <dt>MACs per vector op</dt><dd class="lo">6.4</dd>
          <dt>vector ops per 64x128 tile</dt><dd>1,280</dd>
          <dt>horizontal reductions, this node</dt><dd class="lo">163,840</dd>
        </dl>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="pull">
      <p>
        A <code>vwredsum</code> is a serial tree. Doing 80 of them per output row is the single
        biggest thing wrong with this kernel, and no amount of tuning inside the loop removes
        it. <strong>The layout has to change.</strong>
      </p>
    </div>
  </div>
</section>

<!-- ============ STAGE 02 ============ -->
<section class="sec" id="s02">
  <div class="wrap">
    <div class="stage-head">
      <div class="stage-num">02</div>
      <div class="stage-titles">
        <p class="stage-kicker">Repack, standard RVV — block_q1_0x64</p>
        <h2>Put 64 rows in the lanes and the reductions disappear</h2>
        <div class="stage-cyc">
          <span class="chip win">decode <b>2,144,213</b>  2.09x</span>
          <span class="chip win">prefill <b>1,696,704</b>  5.23x</span>
          <span class="chip">0 horizontal reductions</span>
        </div>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="beats">
      <div class="beat sym">
        <p class="bt">Symptom</p>
        <p>32 of 128 lanes busy, and 163,840 serial reductions in this one node.</p>
      </div>
      <div class="beat chg">
        <p class="bt">Change</p>
        <p>Transpose the sign bits at load time so lane <em>j</em> holds <b>row j</b>, not column j.</p>
      </div>
      <div class="beat eff">
        <p class="bt">Effect</p>
        <p><span class="big">2.09x</span>The reduction over K becomes a vertical add inside each lane. Zero horizontal reductions remain.</p>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="prose" style="margin-top:1.8rem">
      <p>
        Turn the tile 90 degrees. If each lane owns one output row, then summing over the K
        dimension is just adding into that lane over and over — a loop-carried vertical
        add, which costs nothing extra.
      </p>
      <p>
        For that to work the bits have to be rearranged so that <strong>one mask load gives one
        column across all 64 rows</strong>. That is the repacked block: the same 1152 bytes as
        64 original blocks, permuted. No weight data is added or removed.
      </p>
    </div>

    <div class="panels">
      <div class="panel">
        <div class="panel-label"><span>Repacked layout — block_q1_0x64</span><span class="r">1152 B = 64 x 18 B</span></div>
        <div class="bytemap">
          <div class="bseg d" style="flex:128"><span>d[64]</span><span class="n">128 B</span></div>
          <div class="bseg q hi" style="flex:64"><span>plane 0</span><span class="n">8 B</span></div>
          <div class="bseg q" style="flex:64"><span>plane 1</span><span class="n">8 B</span></div>
          <div class="bseg q striped" style="flex:832"><span>planes 2 .. 127</span><span class="n">8 B each</span></div>
        </div>
        <div class="bytemap-key"><span>byte 0</span><span>byte 1151</span></div>
        <p class="cap">
          <b>Bit index <code>c*64 + j</code>.</b> Plane <em>c</em> is 64 contiguous row bits for
          column <em>c</em>, so one 8-byte <code>vlm</code> loads a whole column as an RVV mask
          — exactly the operand the masked add wants.
        </p>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="panels wide-left">
      <div class="panel">
        <div class="panel-label"><span>What one step touches</span><span class="r">64 rows x 1 column</span></div>
        <div class="gridbox">
          <div class="gridwrap">
            <div class="xlab"><span>col c</span><span>c+15 of 128</span></div>
            <div class="ylab"><span>row 0</span><span>row 63</span></div>
            <div class="lanegrid dim" data-rows="64" data-cols="16" data-seed="11"
                 data-hl="col" data-hl-start="5" data-hl-span="1" data-hl-tag="1 vlm = 64 rows"></div>
          </div>
        </div>
        <div class="legend">
          <span><i class="p"></i> weight +1</span>
          <span><i class="m"></i> weight -1</span>
          <span><i class="k"></i> one inner-loop step</span>
        </div>
        <p class="cap">
          Every lane is now an output row. The step advances one column and all 64 accumulators
          move together.
        </p>
      </div>

      <div class="panel">
        <div class="panel-label"><span>Inner loop</span><span class="r">per column</span></div>
        <div class="ops"><span class="cm">; sumi is i16, 64 lanes; y is a scalar int8</span>
<span class="op">vlm.v   </span>  v0, (plane c)   <span class="cm">; 64 row bits</span>
<span class="op">vsub.vx </span>  v8, v8, y       <span class="cm">; -y everywhere</span>
<span class="op">vadd.vx </span>  v8, v8, 2y, v0.t <span class="cm">; +2y where set</span>
<span class="cm">; net effect: +y or -y, per lane, per column</span></div>
        <dl class="tally">
          <dt>lanes busy</dt><dd class="hi">64 of 64 rows</dd>
          <dt>MACs per vector op</dt><dd class="hi">21.3</dd>
          <dt>vector ops per 64x128 tile</dt><dd>384</dd>
          <dt>horizontal reductions</dt><dd class="hi">0</dd>
        </dl>
        <p class="cap">
          LMUL follows VLEN so the 64 fp32 accumulators exactly fill the machine: i16 m1 / f32 m2
          at VLEN=1024, i16 m2 / f32 m4 at VLEN=512.
        </p>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="cards c2">
      <div class="card">
        <p class="tagline">Constraint solved</p>
        <h3>No zvfh needed</h3>
        <p>
          The 64 fp16 row scales are expanded to fp32 with plain integer bit math, and the int16
          group sums are widened with <code>vsext</code> + <code>vfcvt</code> rather than
          <code>vfwcvt.f.x.v</code>, which some RTLs reject. The kernel runs on a
          <code>zve32f</code> machine.
        </p>
      </div>
      <div class="card">
        <p class="tagline">The gate this creates</p>
        <h3>Rows must be a multiple of 64</h3>
        <p>
          64 rows per lane group means a tensor whose row count is not divisible by 64 cannot be
          repacked, and silently falls back to the stage 01 kernel. In this model exactly one
          tensor fails: the LM head, <code>[2560 x 151669]</code>, because 151669 mod 64 = 53.
        </p>
      </div>
    </div>

    <p class="nextup"><b>New bottleneck</b>
      The arithmetic is now nearly free, which exposes what was hidden behind it. The gemv
      streams 1152 fresh bytes per block and never reuses any of them, so the kernel spends its
      time waiting for memory.
    </p>
  </div>
</section>

<!-- ============ STAGE 03 ============ -->
<section class="sec" id="s03">
  <div class="wrap">
    <div class="stage-head">
      <div class="stage-num">03</div>
      <div class="stage-titles">
        <p class="stage-kicker">Software prefetch — zicbop</p>
        <h2>Ask for the next block before you need it</h2>
        <div class="stage-cyc">
          <span class="chip win">decode <b>1,389,236</b>  1.54x over 02</span>
          <span class="chip">prefill 1,651,949  1.03x</span>
          <span class="chip">results unchanged</span>
        </div>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="beats">
      <div class="beat sym">
        <p class="bt">Symptom</p>
        <p>Decode stalls on weight loads. Each block is 18 cache lines, read once, never reused.</p>
      </div>
      <div class="beat chg">
        <p class="bt">Change</p>
        <p>At the top of block <em>l</em>, issue 18 <code>prefetch.r</code> hints for block <em>l+1</em>.</p>
      </div>
      <div class="beat eff">
        <p class="bt">Effect</p>
        <p><span class="big">1.54x</span>on decode. Prefill barely moves, because its four-row tile already hid the stall.</p>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="panels two">
      <div class="panel">
        <div class="panel-label"><span>Why the hardware cannot do it</span></div>
        <p class="cap" style="margin-top:0">
          The core's hardware prefetcher is shallow by design: <b>4 D-cache prefetch entries</b>
          and L3 line prefetch disabled. With no L2 behind the 32 KB L1, it cannot run far
          enough ahead to cover an L3 or DRAM round trip on a stream this wide.
        </p>
        <div class="ops" style="margin-top:1rem"><span class="cm">; top of block l, 18 lines of block l+1</span>
<span class="op">for</span> o <span class="op">in</span> 0, 64, ..., 1088:
    <span class="hot">prefetch.r</span>  (&bx[l+1] + o)</div>
        <p class="cap">Pure hint. The numbers coming out of the kernel do not change at all.</p>
      </div>

      <div class="panel">
        <div class="panel-label"><span>Distance sweep</span><span class="r">decode, attn_v</span></div>
        <div class="tablewrap" style="margin-top:0;border:0">
          <table style="min-width:0">
            <tbody>
              <tr><td>DIST=0 (off)</td><td>2,144,213</td><td>1.00x</td></tr>
              <tr><td>DIST=1</td><td class="win">1,391,650</td><td class="win">1.54x</td></tr>
              <tr><td>DIST=2</td><td>worse</td><td></td></tr>
              <tr><td>DIST=4</td><td>worse</td><td></td></tr>
            </tbody>
          </table>
        </div>
        <p class="cap">
          One block ahead already hides the latency; looking further only adds cache and MSHR
          pressure. This is why the number was swept rather than assumed.
        </p>
      </div>
    </div>

    <p class="nextup"><b>New bottleneck</b>
      Memory is covered, so what is left is instructions. Even with all 64 lanes busy, one
      vector op still only retires 21 multiply-adds — because each op handles a single
      column.
    </p>
  </div>
</section>

<!-- ============ STAGE 04 ============ -->
<section class="sec" id="s04">
  <div class="wrap">
    <div class="stage-head">
      <div class="stage-num">04</div>
      <div class="stage-titles">
        <p class="stage-kicker">Andes V5 XAndesVDot — nds.vd4dots.vv</p>
        <h2>One instruction, 256 multiply-accumulates</h2>
        <div class="stage-cyc">
          <span class="chip win">decode <b>457,092</b>  3.04x over 03</span>
          <span class="chip win">prefill <b>931,754</b>  1.77x</span>
          <span class="chip">bit-identical to 03</span>
        </div>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="beats">
      <div class="beat sym">
        <p class="bt">Symptom</p>
        <p>One vector op per column. 21 MACs retired per instruction, and four load operations
          per 32 bytes of mask.</p>
      </div>
      <div class="beat chg">
        <p class="bt">Change</p>
        <p>Permute the bits once more so <b>four columns</b> fit one register group, and use the
          core's own 4-way dot instruction.</p>
      </div>
      <div class="beat eff">
        <p class="bt">Effect</p>
        <p><span class="big">3.04x</span>64 MACs per vector op, and a quarter as many mask loads
          for the same bytes.</p>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="prose" style="margin-top:1.8rem">
      <p>
        <code>nds.vd4dots.vv</code> is a <strong>stock Andes vendor instruction</strong> on this
        core, not a custom extension we had to design. At <code>e32</code> it computes, for
        every 32-bit lane:
      </p>
    </div>

    <div class="ops" style="max-width:62ch;margin-top:.4rem"><span class="hot">vd[j] += vs1[4j+0]*vs2[4j+0] + vs1[4j+1]*vs2[4j+1]
        + vs1[4j+2]*vs2[4j+2] + vs1[4j+3]*vs2[4j+3]</span>
<span class="cm">; int8 x int8 accumulated into the i32 lane
; vd, vs1, vs2 all at the same LMUL</span></div>

    <div class="prose" style="margin-top:1.2rem">
      <p>
        Here is the piece of luck that made this stage work. At VLEN=1024,
        <code>e32/m2</code> is exactly <strong>64 i32 lanes = 64 rows</strong>, and that same
        register group seen as bytes is <strong>256 bytes = 64 rows x 4 columns</strong>. The
        instruction's operand shape and our repacked tile are <em>the same object</em>. All that
        was left was to make the bits arrive in that order.
      </p>
    </div>

    <div class="panels">
      <div class="panel">
        <div class="panel-label"><span>The operand shape</span><span class="r">8 of 64 lanes shown</span></div>
        <div class="scrollx">
          <div class="regrow">
            <span class="regname"><b>v12</b> weights, i8 view</span>
            <span class="lanes" data-reg="w" data-lanes="8" data-seed="23"></span>
            <span class="ellip">... 64 lanes</span>
          </div>
          <div class="regrow">
            <span class="regname"><b>v16</b> activations, i8 view</span>
            <span class="lanes" data-reg="a" data-lanes="8" data-seed="5"></span>
            <span class="ellip">same 4 quants in every lane</span>
          </div>
          <div class="collapse" data-collapse="8"></div>
          <div class="regrow">
            <span class="regname"><b>v8</b> accumulator, i32 view</span>
            <span class="lanes" data-reg="acc" data-lanes="8"></span>
            <span class="ellip">one row per lane</span>
          </div>
        </div>
        <p class="cap">
          Lane <em>j</em> is output row <em>j</em>. Its four bytes are that row's four
          consecutive K columns. One instruction retires <b>64 rows x 4 columns = 256 MACs</b>.
        </p>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="panels wide-left">
      <div class="panel">
        <div class="panel-label"><span>Layout, permuted again</span><span class="r">same 1152 B</span></div>
        <div class="bytemap">
          <div class="bseg d" style="flex:128"><span>d[64]</span><span class="n">128 B</span></div>
          <div class="bseg q hi" style="flex:256"><span>plane 0 — columns 0..3</span><span class="n">32 B = 256 bits</span></div>
          <div class="bseg q striped" style="flex:768"><span>planes 1 .. 31</span><span class="n">32 B each</span></div>
        </div>
        <div class="bytemap-key"><span>byte 0</span><span>byte 1151</span></div>
        <p class="cap">
          <b>Bit index <code>(c/4)*256 + 4*j + (c%4)</code>.</b> A plane now covers four columns.
          Bit <code>4j + (c%4)</code> is byte lane <code>4j + (c%4)</code> of the register group
          — the position the dot reads for row <em>j</em>, column <em>c</em>. Same bytes as
          stage 02, only permuted.
        </p>
        <div class="scrollx" style="margin-top:1rem">
          <div class="regrow">
            <span class="regname"><b>one vlm</b> 32 B mask</span>
            <span class="lanes" data-reg="nib" data-lanes="8" data-seed="23"></span>
            <span class="ellip">... 64 nibbles</span>
          </div>
        </div>
        <p class="cap">
          Read as 64 nibbles: nibble <em>j</em> is row <em>j</em>, and its four bits are columns
          c..c+3. A single <code>vmerge</code> turns the whole mask into 256 bytes of +1 / -1.
        </p>
      </div>

      <div class="panel">
        <div class="panel-label"><span>Inner loop</span><span class="r">per 4 columns</span></div>
        <div class="ops"><span class="op">vlm.v         </span> v0, (plane c/4) <span class="cm">; 32 B</span>
<span class="op">vmerge.vxm    </span> v12, vneg1, 1, v0
<span class="op">vmv.v.x       </span> v16, a          <span class="cm">; 4 quants</span>
<span class="hot">nds.vd4dots.vv</span> v8, v12, v16   <span class="cm">; 256 MACs</span></div>
        <dl class="tally">
          <dt>lanes busy</dt><dd class="hi">64 rows x 4 cols</dd>
          <dt>MACs per vector op</dt><dd class="hi">64.0</dd>
          <dt>vector ops per 64x128 tile</dt><dd class="hi">128</dd>
          <dt>mask loads per block</dt><dd class="hi">32 x 32 B</dd>
          <dt>  was, stage 02</dt><dd>128 x 8 B</dd>
        </dl>
        <p class="cap">
          Same bytes, <b>a quarter of the load operations</b>. That is why the in-model win
          (3.04x) beats the standalone cache-resident lab (2.52x) — the lab could not see
          the load traffic.
        </p>
      </div>
    </div>

    <h3 style="margin-top:2.6rem">The same instruction, tiled two ways</h3>
    <div class="prose" style="margin-top:.6rem">
      <p>
        Decode multiplies by one activation vector, prefill by four at once. The dot is used the
        same way in both, but <strong>which operand gets reused flips</strong> — and that
        decides how the 32 vector registers are budgeted.
      </p>
    </div>

    <div class="panels two">
      <div class="panel">
        <div class="panel-label"><span>gemv / decode</span><span class="r">q1_vd4dots_x4_m2</span></div>
        <div class="scrollx">
          <div class="regrow">
            <span class="regname">weights</span>
            <span class="lanes" data-reg="tile" data-tiles="4" data-labels="w0,w1,w2,w3"></span>
          </div>
          <div class="regrow">
            <span class="regname">activations</span>
            <span class="lanes" data-reg="tile" data-tiles="4" data-labels="a0,a1,a2,a3" data-kind="a"></span>
          </div>
          <div class="regrow">
            <span class="regname">accumulator</span>
            <span class="lanes" data-reg="tile" data-tiles="1" data-labels="acc" data-kind="acc" data-w="4"></span>
          </div>
        </div>
        <p class="cap">
          <b>Four different columns, one accumulator.</b> Four dots are chained into the same
          register so the pipeline stays fed while each result is still in flight.
        </p>
      </div>

      <div class="panel">
        <div class="panel-label"><span>gemm / prefill</span><span class="r">q1_vd4dots_4acc_m2</span></div>
        <div class="scrollx">
          <div class="regrow">
            <span class="regname">weights</span>
            <span class="lanes" data-reg="tile" data-tiles="1" data-labels="w" data-w="4"></span>
          </div>
          <div class="regrow">
            <span class="regname">activations</span>
            <span class="lanes" data-reg="tile" data-tiles="4" data-labels="a0,a1,a2,a3" data-kind="a"></span>
          </div>
          <div class="regrow">
            <span class="regname">accumulators</span>
            <span class="lanes" data-reg="tile" data-tiles="4" data-labels="acc0,acc1,acc2,acc3" data-kind="acc"></span>
          </div>
        </div>
        <p class="cap">
          <b>One weight vector, four output rows.</b> The weight stream is read once and used
          four times, which is why prefill was already efficient before stage 03 and gained
          almost nothing from prefetching.
        </p>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="cards c3">
      <div class="card">
        <p class="tagline">One authority</p>
        <h3>The layout cannot drift</h3>
        <p>
          Both bit orders live in one function, <code>q1_0x64_sign_bit()</code>. The repack
          writer and every reader call it. A numeric test can never catch a layout mistake here
          — writer and reader would share the bug, so it cancels. Only a codegen gate can.
        </p>
      </div>
      <div class="card">
        <p class="tagline">gemv activation side</p>
        <h3>Restage, do not gather</h3>
        <p>
          The dot wants 4 activation quants as one 32-bit element, but <code>block_q8_0</code>
          puts <code>qs</code> at offset 2, so every other group sits at 2 mod 4 and the core
          faults on a misaligned 32-bit vector element load. Copy the quants once per call
          through byte load/store (EEW=8 has no alignment rule). Under 1%.
        </p>
      </div>
      <div class="card">
        <p class="tagline">gemm activation side</p>
        <h3>De-interleave with vnsrl</h3>
        <p>
          The 4-row activation block stores <code>qs[c*4 + m]</code>, but row <em>m</em> needs
          its four columns contiguous — a stride-4 gather. Instead peel the byte lanes
          apart once per row tile with <code>vnsrl</code> (u32 to 2x u16 to 4x u8): 6 shifts and
          4 stores per 32 columns, reused by every column tile.
        </p>
      </div>
    </div>

    <p class="nextup"><b>New bottleneck</b>
      With the dot in place, the loop body is small enough that its overhead is visible. Reading
      the generated assembly showed <b>40% of the gemv's inner loop was not arithmetic at
      all</b>.
    </p>
  </div>
</section>

<!-- ============ STAGE 05 ============ -->
<section class="sec" id="s05">
  <div class="wrap">
    <div class="stage-head">
      <div class="stage-num">05</div>
      <div class="stage-titles">
        <p class="stage-kicker">Codegen — the vtype churn</p>
        <h2>Forty percent of the loop was changing element width</h2>
        <div class="stage-cyc">
          <span class="chip win">decode <b>362,799</b>  1.26x over 04</span>
          <span class="chip win">prefill <b>818,314</b>  1.14x</span>
          <span class="chip">the math did not change at all</span>
        </div>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="beats">
      <div class="beat sym">
        <p class="bt">Symptom</p>
        <p><b>Four <code>vsetvli</code> per dot</b> in the gemv. They do no arithmetic; they only
          re-describe the registers.</p>
      </div>
      <div class="beat chg">
        <p class="bt">Change</p>
        <p>Put every 32-bit operation, broadcasts included, inside <b>one inline asm block</b> so
          the compiler only has byte-width work left to schedule.</p>
      </div>
      <div class="beat eff">
        <p class="bt">Effect</p>
        <p><span class="big">1.26x</span>decode, 1.14x prefill, from 4.00 down to 0.94
          <code>vsetvli</code> per dot. Not one line of math was touched.</p>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="prose" style="margin-top:1.8rem">
      <p>
        The kernel keeps switching between two views of the same registers: the <strong>byte
        view</strong> for the mask load and sign expand, and the <strong>32-bit view</strong> for
        the broadcast and the dot. Every switch needs a <code>vsetvli</code>. GCC makes it worse:
        it cannot see inside an inline asm block, so it assumes each one left <code>vtype</code>
        unknown and re-issues its own on top.
      </p>
    </div>

    <div class="panels two">
      <div class="panel">
        <div class="panel-label"><span>Before</span><span class="r">4.00 vsetvli per dot</span></div>
        <div class="ops"><span class="bad">vsetvli</span> e8       <span class="cm">; byte view</span>
<span class="op">vlm.v  </span> v0
<span class="op">vmerge </span> v12
<span class="bad">vsetvli</span> e32      <span class="cm">; 32-bit view</span>
<span class="op">vmv.v.x</span> v16
<span class="hot">nds.vd4dots.vv</span> v8, v12, v16
<span class="bad">vsetvli</span> e32      <span class="cm">; GCC re-issues</span>
<span class="bad">vsetvli</span> e8       <span class="cm">; next column</span>
<span class="cm">; ... repeat, once per single dot</span></div>
      </div>
      <div class="panel">
        <div class="panel-label"><span>After</span><span class="r">0.94 vsetvli per dot</span></div>
        <div class="ops"><span class="op">vsetvli</span> e8       <span class="cm">; once for 4 columns</span>
<span class="op">vlm.v  </span> v0 x4
<span class="op">vmerge </span> v12 x4
<span class="cm">; one asm block, everything e32 inside:</span>
<span class="hot">vsetvli</span> e32, m2
<span class="op">vmv.v.x</span> s0 ; <span class="op">vmv.v.x</span> s1
<span class="hot">nds.vd4dots.vv</span> acc, w0, s0
<span class="hot">nds.vd4dots.vv</span> acc, w1, s1
<span class="op">vmv.v.x</span> s0 ; <span class="op">vmv.v.x</span> s1
<span class="hot">nds.vd4dots.vv</span> acc, w2, s0
<span class="hot">nds.vd4dots.vv</span> acc, w3, s1</div>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="tablewrap">
      <table>
        <caption>Static count, -O3, between the first and last dot</caption>
        <thead>
          <tr><th>Kernel</th><th>vsetvli / dot, before</th><th>after</th><th>instrs / dot, before</th><th>after</th></tr>
        </thead>
        <tbody>
          <tr><td>gemv</td><td>4.00</td><td class="win">0.94</td><td>10.00</td><td class="win">7.90</td></tr>
          <tr><td>gemm</td><td>2.00</td><td class="win">0.52</td><td>9.00</td><td class="win">4.13</td></tr>
        </tbody>
      </table>
    </div>

    <div class="cards c2">
      <div class="card trap">
        <p class="tagline">Did not work</p>
        <h3>Grouping the two widths in the source</h3>
        <p>
          Writing all four mask loads first and all four dots after only got the gemv from 4.00
          to 2.00. The scheduler interleaves them again. The fix has to be inside a single asm
          block, where the scheduler cannot reach.
        </p>
      </div>
      <div class="card trap">
        <p class="tagline">Did not work</p>
        <h3>Four scratch registers instead of two</h3>
        <p>
          The idea was to double the distance between each broadcast and the dot that consumes
          it. No spills, 4.06 instructions per dot instead of 4.13 — and <b>4.5%
          slower</b> (855,476 versus 818,314). Producer-consumer distance is not what limits the
          gemm. Reverted.
        </p>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="pull">
      <p>
        After this stage the two paths are bound by different things. Cycles per issued
        instruction: the gemv went 2.23 to 2.24 — <strong>unchanged</strong>, so it is
        purely instruction-issue bound and every instruction removed became a cycle saved, one
        for one. The gemm went 2.53 to <strong>4.84</strong>. It is no longer issue bound:
        roughly 11 cycles per dot are stall, and cutting more instructions will not help
        prefill.
      </p>
    </div>
  </div>
</section>

<!-- ============ TRAPS ============ -->
<section class="sec" id="traps">
  <div class="wrap">
    <div class="sec-head">
      <p class="eyebrow">Also shipped</p>
      <h2>Three traps that delete the win, silently</h2>
      <div class="prose">
        <p>
          Each of these produced <em>correct results</em> while removing the optimization, so no
          numeric test could ever see it. Each one now has a comment in the source and a script
          that fails the build.
        </p>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="cards c3">
      <div class="card trap">
        <p class="tagline">Trap 01 — 18x</p>
        <h3>The stride-0 broadcast</h3>
        <p>
          Handed "load a word, then splat it", GCC contracts the pair into
          <code>vlse32.v vd,(rs1),zero</code>. A stride-0 strided load is <b>element-serial</b>
          on this core. Since stage 05 the broadcast is written by hand as <code>vmv.v.x</code>
          inside the asm block, taking the quads as plain GPRs, so the contraction is impossible.
        </p>
      </div>
      <div class="card trap">
        <p class="tagline">Trap 02 — fault</p>
        <h3>Misaligned vector element load</h3>
        <p>
          The core faults on a misaligned 32-bit vector element load. <code>block_q8_0</code>
          puts <code>qs</code> at offset 2 and is 34 bytes, so every other group is 2 mod 4.
          Restaging through byte load/store fixes it; the 4-row activation block is 4-byte
          aligned and needs no restaging.
        </p>
      </div>
      <div class="card trap">
        <p class="tagline">Trap 03 — silent DCE</p>
        <h3>always_inline is load-bearing</h3>
        <p>
          A prefetch has no observable effect, so whenever the compiler leaves the helper out of
          line, <code>ipa-pure-const</code> marks it pure and dead-code elimination deletes every
          call. No warning, results still correct. GCC 14.2 does exactly this at
          <code>-Os</code>, which had silently removed the entire stage 03 win from the
          MinSizeRel build.
        </p>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="panels two">
      <div class="panel">
        <div class="panel-label"><span>check-vd4dots.sh</span><span class="r">at -O2, -O3, -Os</span></div>
        <div class="ops"><span class="cm">; per KERNEL, not per entry point -</span>
<span class="cm">; the d4 kernels stay out of line</span>
nds.vd4dots  > 0   <span class="cm">; else it fell back, 3x slow</span>
prefetch.r   > 0   <span class="cm">; trap 03</span>
vsetvli/dot <= 1   <span class="cm">; stage 05 budget</span>
vlse*       == 0   <span class="cm">; trap 01</span></div>
        <p class="cap">
          It rewrites the build's own compile line out of <code>compile_commands.json</code>, so
          the gate tests the flags the build actually uses.
        </p>
      </div>
      <div class="panel">
        <div class="panel-label"><span>test-repack-q1_0</span><span class="r">13 cases x 2 layouts</span></div>
        <p class="cap" style="margin-top:0">
          Two of the thirteen exist only because they are the only shapes where the gemm's
          row-tile loop advances more than once, so they are the only ones that check the
          activation and output strides. Proved by fault injection: swapping two rows in the
          de-interleave fails exactly those two and nothing else.
        </p>
        <p class="cap">
          Stages 03, 04 and 05 are <b>bit-identical</b> to stage 02 — every error figure is
          unchanged, not merely within tolerance.
        </p>
      </div>
    </div>
  </div>
</section>

<!-- ============ RESULTS ============ -->
<section class="sec" id="results">
  <div class="wrap">
    <div class="sec-head">
      <p class="eyebrow">Measured</p>
      <h2>Every Q1_0 node in one layer</h2>
      <div class="prose">
        <p>
          The headline number comes from the smallest matmul in the model, so the obvious
          question is whether it generalizes. Layer 7 contains <strong>all six distinct Q1_0
          shapes</strong>, across a 9.5x range of node size. Each one was measured separately.
        </p>
        <p>
          The win is <strong>shape-invariant</strong>: 3.03x to 3.16x from the dot on every
          single one.
        </p>
      </div>
    </div>

    <div class="tablewrap">
      <table>
        <caption>Decode / gemv, nrows=2, cycles</caption>
        <thead>
          <tr>
            <th>Node</th><th>Shape</th>

            <th>04 / 03</th><th>04 / 01</th>
          </tr>

          <tr><td>attn_output</td><td>4096x2560</td><td>18,316,032</td><td>5,492,936</td><td>1,777,405</td><td class="win">3.09x</td><td class="win">10.31x</td></tr>
          <tr><td>ffn_gate</td><td>2560x9728</td><td>42,178,724</td><td>12,997,485</td><td>4,118,497</td><td class="win">3.16x</td><td class="win">10.24x</td></tr>
          <tr><td>ffn_up</td><td>2560x9728</td><td>42,134,940</td><td>12,997,000</td><td>4,118,579</td><td class="win">3.16x</td><td class="win">10.23x</td></tr>
          <tr><td>ffn_down</td><td>9728x2560</td><td>49,054,708</td><td>12,997,483</td><td>4,284,663</td><td class="win">3.03x</td><td class="win">11.45x</td></tr>
